title: Caterpillars: Nature's Magicians
summary: Josh and Chuck explore caterpillars as the larval stage of moths and butterflies: their eating-focused life, molting through five instars, body structure (true legs vs. prolegs, muscles, spiracles, hemolymph), movement (inchworm and wave motion), vision, setae and their irritating effects, defensive tactics (frass shooting, silk drop-offs, camouflage, feeding under leaves), gregarious species and silk trails, pupation into chrysalis or cocoon, complete metamorphosis via imaginal cells over about two weeks, the Hawaiian snail-eating caterpillars, dangerous species like the assassin caterpillar and puss caterpillar, Eastern tent caterpillars and horse reproductive loss syndrome, and gardening management including Bt. The episode closes with a listener mail about a crossword constructor and a plug for tour dates and a possible butterfly two-parter.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening
segments.summary: Hosts promote the final 2023 tour dates in Orlando, Nashville and Atlanta and the show's website and ticket links.

segments.title: Opening banter on caterpillars
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, credit Tracy Wilson's insect articles, and note that caterpillars and butterflies are the same species at different life stages.

segments.title: Caterpillar as larval stage
segments.summary: A caterpillar is the larval stage of a moth or butterfly, whose life is spent eating and molting. Its body is built as an eating machine and storage for fat, and it can eat many times its body size.

segments.title: Eggs and molting
segments.summary: Caterpillars eat their way out of the egg and grow to about one hundred times their size by pupation. They molt five times, triggered by a hormone and enzyme that release the old skin.

segments.title: Caterpillar memory
segments.summary: Researchers at Georgetown reportedly trained caterpillars to avoid smells, and the adult butterflies still avoided those smells.

segments.title: Caterpillar body, legs, muscles, senses and breathing
segments.summary: Caterpillars have six true legs and many prolegs with crochet hooks, about 4,000 muscles, and move by crawling or inchworm-style arching. They have stemmata that detect light and dark, are colorblind, breathe through spiracles and tracheae, and have hemolymph that carries hormones rather than oxygen.

segments.title: Setae and caterpillar hairs
segments.summary: Caterpillar hairs and spines, called setae, can carry irritants and toxins that cause bumps or pain when touched.

segments.title: Touching caterpillars and carnivorous Hawaiian caterpillars
segments.summary: Hosts recall childhood handling of caterpillars. Some Hawaiian caterpillars are carnivores that tie snails to twigs with silk and eat them, while an Australian species eats ants.

segments.title: Caterpillar camouflage and snake mimicry
segments.summary: Caterpillars use leaves for camouflage and some have eye spots that resemble snakes. Gregarious groups can line up to look like a long snake.

segments.title: Caterpillar defenses
segments.summary: Defenses include shooting frass (poop) up to five feet, as with the silver-spotted skipper, nibbling many leaves to hide their presence, and spinning silk lines to drop off from predators.

segments.title: Silk use and gregarious communities
segments.summary: Caterpillars use silk as climbing rope, lassos and nests, and gregarious species build large tents and silk trails reused across generations. Living in groups has trade-offs in shelter and food versus competition and disease.

segments.title: Pupation and chrysalis versus cocoon
segments.summary: After the fifth molt, caterpillars wander off, hang upside down and form a chrysalis from hardened skin. Moths spin a cocoon instead. Silk anchors the pupa in various ways.

segments.title: Inside the chrysalis
segments.summary: Time-lapse photography shows the transformation inside the chrysalis without harming the caterpillar. Silk is used to hang and stabilize the pupa.

segments.title: How metamorphosis works
segments.summary: The caterpillar breaks down into a cell soup; some cells, like leg cells, are rearranged, while others become imaginal cells, similar to stem cells, which form the butterfly over about two weeks. The reason for this evolution is not well understood.

segments.title: Break banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the Josh Clark metamorphosis comment and the break.

segments.title: Pupation duration and temperature
segments.summary: Pupation takes about two weeks on average, longer or shorter depending on weather, and some species overwinter. The ideal temperature is about 21 degrees Celsius, which Josh converts to about 84.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Brief ad break referenced by hosts.

segments.title: Caterpillar management in gardens
segments.summary: Hosts advise against overreacting to a few garden caterpillars, since they are food for birds and pollinators. Gregarious species such as gypsy moths can defoliate trees and damage crops, and egg rings should be removed early. Burning nests is dangerous.

segments.title: Bacillus thuringiensis and organic pest control
segments.summary: Bacillus thuringiensis, sold as an organic caterpillar control, kills caterpillars in general by creating gut holes and sepsis. Hosts express disapproval.

segments.title: Assassin caterpillar and dangerous species
segments.summary: The assassin caterpillar, Lonomia obliqua, in South America has an anticoagulant venom linked to around five hundred deaths and studied for biomedicine; only a couple of species in the genus have this venom. The puss caterpillar in North America causes severe pain, and Eastern tent caterpillars can cause horse reproductive loss syndrome when horses eat them.
